subject: physics

items.q: A body is displaced from its equilibrium position and released. Which condition ensures that it then moves with simple harmonic motion?
items.correct: The resultant force on it is proportional to its displacement and directed towards equilibrium.
items.misconception: A resultant force of constant size acts on it, directed towards the equilibrium position.
items.why: Examiner reports on the definition of SHM repeatedly note answers that mention only "a force towards the centre" and leave out the proportionality. Students picture a restoring force as a pull back to the middle and do not ask how its size varies. SHM requires both conditions: F (and so a) proportional to x, and directed towards equilibrium. With a constant restoring force the body oscillates, but the period depends on the amplitude and the displacement–time graph is not sinusoidal.
items.specStatementText: conditions that lead to simple harmonic motion
items.random_wrong: The resultant force on it is proportional to its displacement and acts in the same direction as it.

items.q: Each option describes a body that can move along a straight line. It gives the resultant force F on the body when it is held at displacements x = +0.020 m, +0.040 m and +0.060 m from its equilibrium position, in that order. At the corresponding negative displacements, F has the same size and the opposite sign. Which body will move with simple harmonic motion when displaced and released?
items.why:
Examiner reports note definitions of SHM that give "acceleration proportional to displacement" without the direction. The phrase "a is proportional to x" is memorised as a slogan and the minus sign in a = −ω²x is treated as a detail. The direction is essential. A force F = +kx grows as the body moves away and drives it further from equilibrium, so there is no oscillation at all. Only F = −kx, always towards equilibrium, gives SHM.

Working: Test each set for F ∝ x and F opposite to x. First set: F/x = −0.30/0.020 = −0.60/0.040 = −0.90/0.060 = −15 N m⁻¹, constant and negative, so F = −15x: SHM. Second: F constant (not ∝ x). Third: F/x = +15 N m⁻¹, force away from equilibrium, no oscillation. Fourth: |F| decreases as x increases, not ∝ x.
items.specStatementText: conditions that lead to simple harmonic motion
items.working: Test each set for F ∝ x and F opposite to x. First set: F/x = −0.30/0.020 = −0.60/0.040 = −0.90/0.060 = −15 N m⁻¹, constant and negative, so F = −15x: SHM. Second: F constant (not ∝ x). Third: F/x = +15 N m⁻¹, force away from equilibrium, no oscillation. Fourth: |F| decreases as x increases, not ∝ x.

items.q: The defining equation of simple harmonic motion is a = −ω²x. What is the significance of the minus sign?
items.correct: The acceleration always points opposite to the displacement, towards the equilibrium position.
items.misconception: The body is slowing down at every point of its motion, as its acceleration is negative.
items.why: At GCSE a negative acceleration is usually introduced as a deceleration, so students attach "slowing down" to the minus sign whatever the direction of motion. Whether a body speeds up or slows down depends on whether a and v have the same or opposite directions. Moving towards equilibrium, a and v are in the same direction and the body speeds up; moving away, they are opposite and it slows down.
items.specStatementText: the defining equation of simple harmonic motion as given by a = −ω²x
items.random_wrong: The oscillation is losing energy, so its amplitude gradually decreases as time passes.

items.q: A body moves with simple harmonic motion along a horizontal line with angular frequency 4.0 rad s⁻¹. Displacements to the right of the equilibrium position are positive. The body is released from rest 0.050 m to the right of the equilibrium position. What is its acceleration when it has moved 0.020 m from the point of release?
items.why:
A procedural error: students meet ω unsquared in ω = 2πf and ω = 2π/T, and carry an unsquared ω into equations in which it is squared. Check units: ω has unit s⁻¹ (rad s⁻¹), so ωx has unit m s⁻¹, a velocity. Only ω²x has the unit of acceleration, m s⁻².

Working: x is measured from equilibrium: x = 0.050 m − 0.020 m = +0.030 m. a = −ω²x = −(4.0 rad s⁻¹)² × (0.030 m) = −16 × 0.030 = −0.48 m s⁻² (0.48 m s⁻² towards the left, towards equilibrium).
items.specStatementText: the defining equation of simple harmonic motion as given by a = −ω²x
items.working: x is measured from equilibrium: x = 0.050 m − 0.020 m = +0.030 m. a = −ω²x = −(4.0 rad s⁻¹)² × (0.030 m) = −16 × 0.030 = −0.48 m s⁻² (0.48 m s⁻² towards the left, towards equilibrium).

items.q: A particle moves with simple harmonic motion. Which statement about the quantities used to describe its motion is correct?
items.correct: Displacement is measured from equilibrium and is negative for half of each cycle.
items.misconception: The amplitude is greatest at each extreme and zero when the particle is at equilibrium.
items.why: Displacement and amplitude are both measured in metres from the same point, and textbooks often label the vertical axis of a displacement–time graph with both, so students use the words interchangeably. Displacement x varies between +x₀ and −x₀ during each cycle; the amplitude x₀ is the fixed size of that variation. The body at equilibrium has zero displacement but the same amplitude as at any other point.
items.specStatementText: a particle undergoing simple harmonic motion can be described using time period T, frequency f, angular frequency ω, amplitude, equilibrium position, and displacement
items.random_wrong: The equilibrium position is where the particle is momentarily at rest in each cycle.

items.q: A glider on a horizontal air track moves with simple harmonic motion alongside a metre rule. It moves back and forth between the 0.20 m mark and the 0.60 m mark on the rule. What are the amplitude and the equilibrium position of the motion?
items.correct: Amplitude 0.20 m; equilibrium position at the 0.40 m mark
items.misconception: Amplitude 0.40 m; equilibrium position at the 0.40 m mark
items.why:
The extremes are the easiest points to see and measure, so the whole width of the swing is taken as "how big" the oscillation is. The same peak-to-peak error is common with wave amplitude. Displacement is measured from equilibrium, so the amplitude is the distance from equilibrium to one extreme. A body moving between marks 0.40 m apart has an amplitude of 0.20 m.

Working: Equilibrium position = midpoint of the extremes = (0.20 m + 0.60 m)/2 = 0.40 m mark. Amplitude = distance from equilibrium to an extreme = 0.60 m − 0.40 m = 0.20 m.
items.specStatementText: a particle undergoing simple harmonic motion can be described using time period T, frequency f, angular frequency ω, amplitude, equilibrium position, and displacement
items.random_wrong: Amplitude 0.60 m; equilibrium position at the 0.40 m mark
items.working: Equilibrium position = midpoint of the extremes = (0.20 m + 0.60 m)/2 = 0.40 m mark. Amplitude = distance from equilibrium to an extreme = 0.60 m − 0.40 m = 0.20 m.

items.q: A body moving with simple harmonic motion passes through its equilibrium position 40 times in 12.0 s. What is its angular frequency?
items.correct: 10.5 rad s⁻¹
items.misconception: 20.9 rad s⁻¹
items.why:
In everyday language one "swing" of a pendulum or a swing seat is the movement from one side to the other, and a pendulum clock ticks once per swing; students count these as complete oscillations. Count one oscillation from a given point back to the same point moving in the same direction. From one extreme to the other is T/2, and the body passes through equilibrium twice in each period.

Working: Two passes through equilibrium per oscillation → 20 oscillations in 12.0 s. T = 12.0 s / 20 = 0.600 s. ω = 2π/T = 2π / 0.600 s = 10.47 rad s⁻¹ ≈ 10.5 rad s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: the time period in terms of frequency of oscillation and angular frequency as given by T = 1/f = 2π/ω
items.random_wrong: 1.67 rad s⁻¹
items.working: Two passes through equilibrium per oscillation → 20 oscillations in 12.0 s. T = 12.0 s / 20 = 0.600 s. ω = 2π/T = 2π / 0.600 s = 10.47 rad s⁻¹ ≈ 10.5 rad s⁻¹.

items.q: A trolley hung from a newton meter gives a reading of 14.7 N. The trolley is then attached to a spring system on a horizontal track and oscillates with negligible friction. The spring constant of the system is 7.50 N m⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the time period of the oscillation?
items.why:
Mass and weight are used interchangeably in everyday speech ("I weigh 60 kilograms"), and the confusion between them is one of the most widely documented in introductory mechanics. Mass (kg) measures inertia; weight (N) is the gravitational force mg. The period depends on inertia, so use m = W/g. A body of weight 14.7 N has a mass of 1.50 kg when g = 9.8 m s⁻².

Working: m = W/g = 14.7 N / 9.8 m s⁻² = 1.50 kg. T = 2π√(m/k) = 2π√(1.50 kg / 7.50 N m⁻¹) = 2π√(0.200 s²) = 2π × 0.447 s = 2.81 s.
items.specStatementText: the time period of a mass–spring system as given by T = 2π√(m/k)

items.q: A body on a spring oscillates with time period T and amplitude A. It is replaced by a body of four times the mass, which is set oscillating on the same spring with amplitude 2A. What happens to the time period?
items.correct: It doubles, as T depends on √m and does not depend on the amplitude.
items.misconception: It quadruples, as T is proportional to m and does not depend on the amplitude.
items.why: Students reason linearly ("more mass, proportionally slower") and drop the square root, a well-documented habit of assuming direct proportion. Keep the square root: multiplying m by 4 multiplies m/k by 4 and √(m/k) by 2. To double the period the mass must be multiplied by 4.
items.specStatementText: the time period of a mass–spring system as given by T = 2π√(m/k)
items.random_wrong: It halves, as T depends on √(k/m), so a larger mass shortens the period.

items.q: The time period of a simple pendulum is given by T = 2π√(l/g). Which condition must be met for this equation to give an accurate value?
items.correct: The amplitude is small, so the restoring force is close to proportional to displacement.
items.misconception: The amplitude can be of any size, since the period is independent of the amplitude.
items.why: The independence of period from amplitude is taught as a key property of SHM, and the small-angle condition on which it depends for a pendulum is easily forgotten. The restoring force on a pendulum bob is mg sin θ, not mgθ. Only for small angles is sin θ ≈ θ, making the force nearly proportional to the displacement and the motion nearly SHM. For large amplitudes the motion is not SHM and the equation underestimates the period.
items.specStatementText: the time period of a simple pendulum as given by T = 2π√(l/g)
items.random_wrong: The bob must be light, as a heavier bob is pulled harder and swings faster than predicted.

items.q: A long simple pendulum hangs in the stairwell of a school. Swinging with a small amplitude, its bob takes 2.10 s to move from one extreme position to the other. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the length of the pendulum?
items.why:
Students reason linearly ("longer string, proportionally slower") and drop the square root. Keep the square root: to double the period the length must be multiplied by 4. When rearranging for l, square both sides: l = gT²/(4π²).

Working: Extreme to extreme = half an oscillation, so T = 2 × 2.10 s = 4.20 s. T = 2π√(l/g) → l = gT²/(4π²) = (9.8 m s⁻²)(4.20 s)² / (4π²) = 172.9 / 39.48 m = 4.38 m.
items.specStatementText: the time period of a simple pendulum as given by T = 2π√(l/g)
items.working: Extreme to extreme = half an oscillation, so T = 2 × 2.10 s = 4.20 s. T = 2π√(l/g) → l = gT²/(4π²) = (9.8 m s⁻²)(4.20 s)² / (4π²) = 172.9 / 39.48 m = 4.38 m.

items.q: A simple pendulum swings with a small amplitude and time period T. Its bob is replaced by one of twice the mass, keeping the same length from the point of suspension to the centre of the bob. The new pendulum is set swinging with twice the original amplitude, which is still small. What is the new time period?
items.correct: It is unchanged at T, as for small amplitudes the period depends only on l and g.
items.misconception: It is less than T, as a heavier bob is pulled more strongly and swings faster.
items.why: The Aristotelian belief that heavier objects fall faster is one of the most persistent documented misconceptions, and students extend it to pendulums: a heavier bob "is pulled harder, so it swings faster". The gravitational restoring force on the bob is proportional to its mass, and so is the bob’s inertia, so the mass cancels, exactly as all bodies fall with the same acceleration in the absence of air resistance. The period depends only on l and g.
items.specStatementText: the time period of a simple pendulum as given by T = 2π√(l/g)
items.random_wrong: It is more than T, as the bob now travels twice as far in each oscillation.

items.q: A mass on a horizontal spring moves with simple harmonic motion on a frictionless surface; air resistance is negligible. Which statement about the energy of the oscillator is correct?
items.correct: At each extreme, all the energy is stored in the spring, because the mass is at rest.
items.misconception: At each extreme, E_k is greatest, because the acceleration of the mass is greatest there.
items.why: Research on students’ understanding of kinematics (e.g. Trowbridge and McDermott) shows velocity and acceleration are commonly conflated: "accelerating" is heard as "going fast". In SHM the two are greatest at different places, which contradicts this intuition. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. At equilibrium the velocity is greatest but momentarily not changing, so a = 0. At an extreme the velocity is zero but changing fastest, so the acceleration is greatest, ω²x₀. Kinetic energy follows the speed, so it too is greatest at equilibrium.
items.specStatementText: a qualitative approach to energy changes during one cycle of an oscillation.
items.random_wrong: At each extreme, the total energy is zero, because the mass is not moving there.

items.q: The displacement of an undamped oscillator varies sinusoidally with time, with time period T. Which statement describes how the kinetic energy of the oscillator varies with time?
items.correct: It is greatest at zero displacement, with two maxima in each period.
items.misconception: It rises and falls once in each period, in step with the displacement.
items.why: Students carry over the shape of the displacement–time graph to every other quantity and do not notice that energy depends on speed (or displacement) regardless of direction. Kinetic energy depends only on the speed, and potential energy only on the distance from equilibrium; neither depends on the direction of motion or on which side of equilibrium the body is. The body passes through equilibrium twice in each cycle, once in each direction, and is at an extreme twice, so each energy reaches its maximum twice per period.
items.specStatementText: a qualitative approach to energy changes during one cycle of an oscillation.
items.random_wrong: It is greatest at each extreme displacement, where the acceleration is greatest.

items.q: Two oscillators, P and Q, each have a time period of 0.80 s. Q reaches its maximum positive displacement 0.20 s after P does. What is the phase difference between P and Q, in radians?
items.correct: 1.57 rad
items.misconception: 0.20 rad
items.why:
The phase difference is measured on a graph against time, so students report the time interval they read off rather than converting it into an angle. Phase difference is an angle, in radians. The same time lag corresponds to different phase differences for oscillations of different period. Divide by T to get the fraction of a cycle, then multiply by 2π.

Working: Fraction of a cycle = Δt/T = 0.20 s / 0.80 s = 0.25. Phase difference Δφ = 2π × 0.25 = π/2 rad = 1.57 rad.
items.specStatementText: that a particle undergoing simple harmonic motion can be described using phase angle
items.random_wrong: 0.25 rad
items.working: Fraction of a cycle = Δt/T = 0.20 s / 0.80 s = 0.25. Phase difference Δφ = 2π × 0.25 = π/2 rad = 1.57 rad.

items.q: The displacement of a particle moving with simple harmonic motion is x = x₀ sin(ωt + φ). At t = 0 the particle passes through its equilibrium position moving in the negative x-direction. What is the phase constant φ?
items.correct: φ = π rad, since sin π = 0 and x becomes negative just after t = 0
items.misconception: φ = 0 rad, as sin 0 = 0 and so the particle starts at equilibrium
items.why:
Students identify the stage of a cycle by position alone, because displacement is what a displacement–time graph shows most directly. Each displacement except ±x₀ is reached twice per cycle, once moving each way, so the phase angle is fixed by displacement and direction of motion together. At equilibrium moving in the positive direction the phase is 0; at equilibrium moving in the negative direction it is π rad.

Working: x(0) = x₀ sin φ = 0 → φ = 0 or π rad. v = ωx₀ cos(ωt + φ); v(0) = ωx₀ cos φ < 0 requires cos φ = −1, so φ = π rad.
items.specStatementText: that a particle undergoing simple harmonic motion can be described using phase angle
items.random_wrong: φ = −π/2 rad, as moving in the negative direction makes x negative, so sin φ = −1
items.working: x(0) = x₀ sin φ = 0 → φ = 0 or π rad. v = ωx₀ cos(ωt + φ); v(0) = ωx₀ cos φ < 0 requires cos φ = −1, so φ = π rad.

items.q: A particle moves with simple harmonic motion with an amplitude of 0.080 m and a time period of 0.50 s. What is its speed when its displacement is 0.050 m?
items.why:
A widespread algebraic error: students treat the square root as distributing over subtraction, as it would over a product. Evaluate x₀² − x² first, then take the square root. √(a² − b²) = a − b only when b = 0 or b = a.

Working: ω = 2π/T = 2π/0.50 s = 12.57 rad s⁻¹. v = ω√(x₀² − x²) = 12.57 × √(0.0064 − 0.0025) m s⁻¹ = 12.57 × √0.0039 = 12.57 × 0.06245 = 0.78 m s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: that problems can be solved using the equations for simple harmonic motion as given by x = x₀ sin(ωt + φ); v = ωx₀ cos(ωt + φ); v = ±ω√(x₀² − x²); E_T = ½mω²x₀²; E_p = ½mω²x².

items.q: A body of mass 0.40 kg moves with simple harmonic motion with angular frequency 5.0 rad s⁻¹ and amplitude 0.12 m. What is its kinetic energy when its displacement is 0.060 m?
items.why:
Students default to direct proportion, a well-documented pattern of linear reasoning, and "halfway" suggests "half the energy". E_p depends on x². At x = x₀/2, E_p = ¼E_T and E_k = ¾E_T. The energies are equal at x = x₀/√2 ≈ 0.71x₀.

Working: E_T = ½mω²x₀² = ½(0.40 kg)(5.0 rad s⁻¹)²(0.12 m)² = 0.072 J. E_p = ½mω²x² = ½(0.40)(25)(0.060)² = 0.018 J. E_k = E_T − E_p = 0.072 J − 0.018 J = 0.054 J = 5.4 × 10⁻² J.
items.specStatementText: that problems can be solved using the equations for simple harmonic motion as given by x = x₀ sin(ωt + φ); v = ωx₀ cos(ωt + φ); v = ±ω√(x₀² − x²); E_T = ½mω²x₀²; E_p = ½mω²x².

items.q: A particle moves with simple harmonic motion with a time period of 2.0 s and an amplitude of 0.050 m. At t = 0 it passes through its equilibrium position moving in the positive direction, so x = x₀ sin ωt. What is its displacement at t = 0.30 s?
items.why:
Students first meet angles and trigonometry in degrees, and calculators are commonly left in degree mode from geometry work. ωt is in radians because ω is in rad s⁻¹. A quarter-cycle phase difference is π/2 rad, not 90. Set the calculator to radian mode before evaluating sin(ωt + φ) or cos(ωt + φ).

Working: ω = 2π/T = 2π/2.0 s = π rad s⁻¹. ωt = π × 0.30 = 0.942 rad (radian mode). x = x₀ sin ωt = 0.050 m × sin(0.942) = 0.050 × 0.809 = 0.0405 m ≈ 4.0 × 10⁻² m.
items.specStatementText: that problems can be solved using the equations for simple harmonic motion as given by x = x₀ sin(ωt + φ); v = ωx₀ cos(ωt + φ); v = ±ω√(x₀² − x²); E_T = ½mω²x₀²; E_p = ½mω²x².

items.q: A mass hanging from a spring oscillates with simple harmonic motion with an angular frequency of 40.0 rad s⁻¹. What is the time period of the oscillation?
items.why:
Both are called "frequency" and both have unit s⁻¹ (rad s⁻¹ and Hz look interchangeable), so students treat them as two names for one quantity. f counts complete oscillations per second; ω counts radians per second, and one oscillation is 2π rad. Always convert with ω = 2πf = 2π/T before using a = −ω²x or the SHM equations.

Working: T = 2π/ω = 2π / (40.0 rad s⁻¹) = 0.1571 s ≈ 0.157 s (3 s.f.). Check: f = ω/2π = 6.37 Hz, and 1/f = 0.157 s.
items.specStatementText: the time period in terms of frequency of oscillation and angular frequency as given by T = 1/f = 2π/ω

items.q: Is every oscillation that repeats with a regular period simple harmonic motion?
items.correct: No. SHM is the particular periodic motion in which the acceleration is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium and directed towards it. Many periodic motions do not meet this condition.
items.misconception: Any motion that repeats back and forth with a regular period is simple harmonic motion.
items.why: Students first meet SHM through pendulums and springs, which are periodic, and "harmonic" sounds like a general word for regular repetition. The defining condition on the acceleration is less memorable than the picture of something swinging. Test the force or acceleration, not the regularity. A ball bouncing vertically on a hard floor, or a ball rolling back and forth in a V-shaped groove, is periodic but not simple harmonic, because its acceleration is not proportional to its displacement from equilibrium.
items.specStatementText: conditions that lead to simple harmonic motion
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the minus sign in a = −ω²x show that the oscillation dies away?
items.correct: No. a = −ω²x describes undamped SHM with constant amplitude. The minus sign gives the direction of the acceleration, not a loss of energy.
items.misconception: The minus sign in a = −ω²x shows that the oscillation loses energy and its amplitude decreases.
items.why: In other equations students meet, such as radioactive decay (dN/dt = −λN) and cooling, a minus sign signals that a quantity is decreasing, so "minus" is read as "dying away". Here the minus sign links two quantities at the same instant: a points opposite to x. The equation contains no term that removes energy; an oscillator obeying it keeps its amplitude for ever. Damping needs an extra resistive force.
items.specStatementText: the defining equation of simple harmonic motion as given by a = −ω²x
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the minus sign in a = −ω²x mean the acceleration is in the negative direction?
items.correct: No. The acceleration is negative when x is positive and positive when x is negative. It always points towards equilibrium.
items.misconception: The minus sign in a = −ω²x means the acceleration always points in the negative direction (for example, to the left or downwards).
items.why: In kinematics a minus sign on a vector labels a fixed direction, such as g = −9.8 m s⁻² for "downwards", so students read the minus sign in a = −ω²x in the same way. x is itself signed. For x > 0, a < 0; for x < 0, a > 0. The minus sign states that a and x are always opposite, so the acceleration reverses direction every time the body passes through equilibrium.
items.specStatementText: the defining equation of simple harmonic motion as given by a = −ω²x
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: From where is the displacement of an oscillator measured?
items.correct: From the equilibrium position, not from the point of release, the end of the motion, or the zero of a measuring scale.
items.misconception: Displacement is measured from a convenient fixed point, such as the point where the body was released or the zero of the measuring scale.
items.why: In kinematics displacement is often measured from the starting point, and in practical work readings are taken from the zero of a ruler, so students do not realise that in SHM the reference point is the equilibrium position. In a = −ω²x, x is measured from the equilibrium position, where the resultant force is zero. A body released 0.050 m from equilibrium that has moved 0.020 m towards it has a displacement of 0.030 m.
items.specStatementText: a particle undergoing simple harmonic motion can be described using time period T, frequency f, angular frequency ω, amplitude, equilibrium position, and displacement
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the equilibrium position where an oscillating body is at rest?
items.correct: No. The equilibrium position is where the resultant force is zero. The oscillating body passes through it at maximum speed; it is momentarily at rest only at the extremes.
items.misconception: The equilibrium position is where the oscillating body is (momentarily) at rest, which is at the extremes of the motion.
items.why: In statics "equilibrium" is taught alongside objects at rest, so students link equilibrium with zero velocity rather than with zero resultant force. Equilibrium means zero resultant force, not zero velocity. At the extremes the velocity is zero but the resultant force is greatest. At the equilibrium position the force is zero and the speed is greatest.
items.specStatementText: a particle undergoing simple harmonic motion can be described using time period T, frequency f, angular frequency ω, amplitude, equilibrium position, and displacement
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is ω found by multiplying 2π by T?
items.correct: No. ω = 2π/T. A longer period means a smaller angular frequency.
items.misconception: The angular frequency is found as ω = 2πT (or the period as T = 2πω).
items.why: A procedural error: ω = 2πf is memorised as "2π times something", and the something is filled with T instead of f. An oscillator with a longer period oscillates more slowly, so ω must decrease as T increases: ω = 2π/T. Check units: 2πT has unit s, not rad s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: the time period in terms of frequency of oscillation and angular frequency as given by T = 1/f = 2π/ω
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a larger mass on a spring oscillate faster?
items.correct: No. A larger mass has more inertia, so the same spring force gives it a smaller acceleration and the period is longer: T = 2π√(m/k).
items.misconception: A larger mass on the spring oscillates faster (shorter period), as though T = 2π√(k/m).
items.why: Students associate "heavier" with "stronger" and "faster", as in the belief that heavier objects fall faster, and the letters m and k are easily swapped inside the square root. For a given displacement the spring exerts the same force whatever the mass, so a larger mass accelerates less and takes longer to complete each cycle. A stiffer spring (larger k), not a larger mass, shortens the period.
items.specStatementText: the time period of a mass–spring system as given by T = 2π√(m/k)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the period of every oscillator independent of the mass?
items.correct: No. The period of a simple pendulum is independent of the bob’s mass, but the period of a mass–spring system depends on the mass: T = 2π√(m/k).
items.misconception: The period of an oscillator does not depend on its mass, just as the period of a simple pendulum does not.
items.why: The mass-independence of the pendulum’s period is taught as a striking result, and students over-generalise it to every oscillator. For a pendulum the restoring force (from gravity) is itself proportional to the mass, so mass cancels. For a spring the restoring force depends only on k and x, not on m, so a larger mass accelerates less and the period grows as √m.
items.specStatementText: the time period of a mass–spring system as given by T = 2π√(m/k)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a pendulum with a larger (small) amplitude take longer for each oscillation?
items.correct: No. For small amplitudes the period does not depend on the amplitude: the bob travels further but, because the restoring force is larger, it moves faster.
items.misconception: A larger amplitude gives a longer period, because the bob has further to travel in each oscillation.
items.why: Everyday reasoning says a longer journey takes longer; students do not take account of the greater speed that the larger restoring force produces. In SHM the restoring force is proportional to the displacement, so doubling the amplitude doubles the maximum acceleration and the maximum speed. Twice the distance at twice the speed takes the same time. T = 2π√(l/g) contains no amplitude.
items.specStatementText: the time period of a simple pendulum as given by T = 2π√(l/g)

items.q: When T = 2π√(l/g) is rearranged for l, what must be squared?
items.correct: The whole of each side must be squared, including the 2π: T/(2π) = √(l/g), so T²/(4π²) = l/g and l = gT²/(4π²).
items.misconception: When the equation is squared to remove the square root, only T needs squaring, giving l = gT²/(2π).
items.why: A procedural error in rearranging: the square root is attached visually to l/g, so students square the T they want to isolate and forget that the 2π must be squared too. Divide by 2π first, then square both sides: (T/2π)² = l/g. The 2π is part of the expression being squared, so it becomes 4π².
items.specStatementText: the time period of a simple pendulum as given by T = 2π√(l/g)

items.q: Is the period of a simple pendulum proportional to the square root of the bob’s mass?
items.correct: No. That is the mass–spring result. For a simple pendulum T = 2π√(l/g), which does not contain the mass.
items.misconception: The period of a simple pendulum is proportional to √m, as it is for a mass on a spring.
items.why: The two period equations are learned together and have the same form, 2π√(…/…), so students transfer the mass dependence of T = 2π√(m/k) to the pendulum. In a mass–spring system the restoring force does not depend on the mass, so mass affects the period. In a pendulum the restoring force is proportional to the mass, which cancels the effect of the larger inertia.
items.specStatementText: the time period of a simple pendulum as given by T = 2π√(l/g)

items.q: Does an oscillator have no energy at the extremes of its motion?
items.correct: No. At the extremes the kinetic energy is zero, but the potential energy is at its maximum and equals the total energy.
items.misconception: An oscillator has energy only when it is moving, so its total energy is greatest at equilibrium and zero at the extremes.
items.why: Research on students’ energy ideas (e.g. Watts; Driver et al.) records the view that energy is associated with activity and movement, so a body at rest is thought to have no energy. Energy is stored as well as carried by motion. At an extreme the spring is most stretched or compressed, or the pendulum bob is highest, so the potential energy is greatest. The sum of kinetic and potential energy is the same at every point.
items.specStatementText: a qualitative approach to energy changes during one cycle of an oscillation.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is energy used up as an undamped oscillator moves?
items.correct: No. With no resistive forces the total energy of the oscillator is constant. Energy is only transferred back and forth between kinetic and potential stores.
items.misconception: Energy is used up in keeping the body moving, so the total energy of an oscillator falls every cycle even when there is no friction or air resistance.
items.why: Everyday language speaks of energy being "used up", and every real oscillator eventually stops, so students assume the loss is part of oscillation itself rather than caused by resistive forces. Energy is conserved. Real oscillators lose energy only because resistive forces transfer it to the surroundings as thermal energy. Without them, kinetic energy lost is exactly potential energy gained, and the total stays constant.
items.specStatementText: a qualitative approach to energy changes during one cycle of an oscillation.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can the kinetic energy of an oscillator be negative?
items.correct: No. Kinetic energy depends on the square of the speed, so it is zero or positive. It is a scalar and has no direction.
items.misconception: Kinetic energy has a direction, so it is negative when the body moves in the negative direction, varying like the velocity.
items.why: Students who have just used signs to show the direction of displacement, velocity and acceleration extend the sign convention to energy, treating it as a vector. Energy is a scalar. When the velocity is negative, v² is still positive. The kinetic energy falls to zero at each extreme and rises to its maximum at equilibrium in both directions of motion.
items.specStatementText: a qualitative approach to energy changes during one cycle of an oscillation.

items.q: Is the phase difference equal to the fraction of a cycle between two oscillations?
items.correct: No. The fraction of a cycle must be multiplied by 2π rad: a quarter of a cycle is π/2 rad.
items.misconception: The phase difference is the fraction of a cycle by which one oscillation leads the other, such as 0.25 for a quarter cycle.
items.why: A procedural error: students correctly find Δt/T but forget that the phase angle is measured in radians, with one cycle = 2π rad. Phase angle measures position in the cycle as an angle, so one whole cycle is 2π rad. Δφ = 2π × (Δt/T).

items.q: Does a body moving in the negative direction have a negative displacement?
items.correct: Not necessarily. The sign of the velocity gives the direction of motion; the sign of the displacement gives the side of equilibrium. A body can be at x = 0 or x > 0 while moving in the negative direction.
items.misconception: A body moving in the negative direction must have a negative displacement, so "moving in the −x direction" means starting at −x₀.
items.why: Research on kinematics graphs (e.g. McDermott et al.) documents students confusing position with velocity, so the sign of one is transferred to the other. Displacement and velocity are separate quantities. In SHM the velocity is greatest at x = 0 and zero at x = ±x₀; at x = 0 the body can be moving either way. At x = −x₀ the body is momentarily at rest.

items.q: Can sine and cosine be swapped in x = x₀ sin(ωt + φ) while keeping the same φ?
items.correct: No. With x = x₀ sin(ωt + φ) and v = ωx₀ cos(ωt + φ), φ = 0 puts the body at equilibrium at t = 0. Replacing sin by cos while keeping the same φ describes a different starting point (an extreme for φ = 0); a cosine form is valid only with φ changed by π/2.
items.misconception: Sine and cosine can be swapped in x = x₀ sin(ωt + φ) without changing φ, so the body's position at t = 0 is the same either way.
items.why: Many textbooks and videos describe SHM with x = x₀ cos ωt (starting from an extreme), so students mix the two forms and apply the wrong one to the IB equation. Use the equation as given: x = x₀ sin(ωt + φ). Check with t = 0 and φ = 0: sin 0 = 0, so the body starts at equilibrium; cos 0 = 1 would put it at an extreme.
items.specStatementText: that problems can be solved using the equations for simple harmonic motion as given by x = x₀ sin(ωt + φ); v = ωx₀ cos(ωt + φ); v = ±ω√(x₀² − x²); E_T = ½mω²x₀²; E_p = ½mω²x².

items.q: Is the speed of an oscillator given by v = ωx?
items.correct: No. v = ±ω√(x₀² − x²). The speed is greatest at equilibrium, where x = 0, and zero at the extremes, the opposite of ωx.
items.misconception: The speed of an oscillator is proportional to its displacement, v = ωx, by analogy with a = −ω²x.
items.why: Students pattern-match with the defining equation, and the conflation of speed with acceleration (both thought to be greatest at the same place) makes v ∝ x seem natural. Speed and displacement are out of step: v is greatest at x = 0 and zero at x = ±x₀. Use v = ±ω√(x₀² − x²), and for energy E_k = ½mω²(x₀² − x²), not ½mω²x², which is E_p.

items.q: Are the frequency and the time period of an oscillation the same quantity?
items.correct: No. The time period T is the time for one complete oscillation, in seconds; the frequency f is the number of oscillations per second, in hertz. They are reciprocals: T = 1/f, so a higher frequency means a shorter period.
items.misconception: Frequency and time period are the same idea, so a value calculated for one can be reported as the other, and a higher frequency goes with a longer time period.
items.why: Both quantities describe 'how fast' an oscillation repeats and are introduced together; the unit hertz is written as s⁻¹, which looks like the unit of period. Surveys of students' understanding of oscillations and waves report that many treat period and frequency as interchangeable or expect them to increase together. Keep the units in view: T is a time, in seconds; f is a rate, in per second (Hz). Check any answer by asking 'is this a time for one oscillation, or a number of oscillations each second?' A fast oscillation has a large f and a small T, since T = 1/f = 2π/ω.
items.specStatementText: the time period in terms of frequency of oscillation and angular frequency as given by T = 1/f = 2π/ω
